title: False friends — same word, different meaning
goal: Uncover the words that are spelled exactly the same in Malaysian Malay and Indonesian but mean different things — you'll hear both meanings in Malaysia, so this is a unit worth reading twice.
bekal: recognize the thirty false friends that trip people up most often
know the four words that aren't just confusing but embarrassing
have a rescue phrase ready for when you realize you've just used the wrong word

notes: **Ni** and **tu** are the spoken forms of *ini* (this) and *itu* (that), and they go **after** the noun: *kertas ni* = this paper, *kereta tu* = that car. Malaysians use the short forms almost all the time in conversation; the full forms sound rather formal.
**Makna / maknanya** (meaning / it means) is the everyday Malaysian word, alongside *maksud / maksudnya*. *Apa maknanya?* = What does it mean?
**Tak payah** = no need, don't bother. *Payah* on its own means "difficult", so *tak payah* is literally "not difficult" — but it has come to mean "no need". *Tak payah bayar* = no need to pay.
**Pelik** = strange, odd. You'll hear it every day. *Pelik betul* = "really weird".
**Alamak** is a typically Malaysian cry of surprise, like "oh no!" or "oh my!". Its cousins: *aiyo*, *adoi*, *ish*, *eh*.

grammars.title: Four words that are more than just confusing
body: Most false friends only raise a smile. The four below are different — getting them wrong can embarrass you or offend the person you're talking to. Learn all four now, before you turn the page.

head: Word
In Malaysia
What to use instead
rows: vulgar word for the male organ (in Indonesian: "to need")
fun, enjoyable (an ordinary word! in Indonesian: obscene)
child (an ordinary word! in Indonesian: slave)

after: Note that the danger runs **both ways**. *Butuh* and *pantat* are dangerous if **you** use them. *Seronok* and *budak* are dangerous if you **misunderstand** them when a Malaysian uses them — and your shocked reaction is what makes things awkward.

The word **punggung** has shifted too: in Malay *punggung* means **bottom, buttocks**, while your back is **belakang**. So *sakit belakang* = backache, and *sakit punggung* = a sore bottom. This comes up at the clinic, so remember it well.

sections.title: The twenty false friends you'll meet most

blocks.text: The full list is at the back of this course. The twenty below are the ones you're most likely to run into in your first week in Malaysia — through Indonesian friends, TV, music or tourists. Learn these first.

The last two deserve a word of their own. **Kerajaan Malaysia** means "the Government of Malaysia" — and since Malaysia really is a monarchy, a sentence like *Kerajaan mengumumkan cukai baru* ("The government announced a new tax") can feel ambiguous until you're used to it. Always: *kerajaan* = government; *istana* (palace) and *raja* (king) = the monarchy. And **panggung wayang** is a cinema — *wayang* here means film, not a puppet show.

sections.title: Words that aren't traps, just different

blocks.text: The second group is much bigger and much friendlier: words that are simply **different** in Malaysia and Indonesia, not same-word-different-meaning. Malaysia says *kedai* for shop, *tandas* for toilet, *beg* for bag, *borang* for form, *cukai* for tax, *hospital* for hospital, where Indonesia uses other words. At worst, using the Indonesian word makes you sound foreign, not embarrassing — and since this course teaches Malaysian Malay, you're already learning the Malaysian set. Just don't assume an unfamiliar word on an Indonesian sign or subtitle is a misprint.

Watch out for **semalam** — it means **yesterday**, not "last night". For "last night" Malaysians say *malam tadi*. And **kelmarin** means **the day before yesterday**. These three are neighbors and easily confused; unit 11 sets them straight.

blocks.title: If you're not sure a word is safe
items: **Perkataan ni maksudnya apa?** — What does this word mean?
**Kat Indonesia maknanya lain.** — In Indonesia it means something else.
**Betul ke saya guna perkataan ni?** — Am I using this word correctly?
**Ada perkataan lain tak?** — Is there another word?
And most useful of all: when in doubt, **use the longer, more formal word**. Standard words almost never turn out to be traps; the dangerous ones are short everyday words.

exercises.prompt: What does the bold word mean in MALAYSIA?

Dia ahli bahasa yang hebat — meaning: an expert.
Saya sakit punggung — meaning: my back hurts.
